archetype.name: Game Manager (veteran spot starter)
archetype.definition: A 14-year journeyman who wins by staying on schedule from structure: timing throws, under-center play-action looks and avoiding sacks, not by creating outside the design or pushing the ball deep.

report.headline: A competent emergency starter whose ceiling depends entirely on a script built for him.
report.take:
Keenum is the Bears' No. 3 quarterback, inactive and serving only as the emergency option, so his 2026 line is a two-game snapshot from when Caleb Williams was out early in the year. It is two very different games. Against Philadelphia, a defense now ranked 27th, he went 24 of 34 for 247 yards and two scores with +7.3 EPA, a 2.8 CPOE and only 8.8% bad throws. In the Green Bay loss, against the ninth-ranked defense on 33% of the snaps, he went 11 of 19 for 108 with an interception, two sacks, a lost fumble, -6.4 EPA and a 31.6% bad-throw rate. The season average of +0.015 EPA per dropback is just those two games netting out. It is not a description of a quarterback who plays at that level every week.

What drove the good version was Ben Johnson's structure. Under center he was +0.818 EPA a play with an 85.7% success rate on 14 plays. From shotgun he was -0.394 on 41. Throws of 10 to 19 yards over the middle were productive: +0.734 a play on intermediate throws and +0.318 a play to the middle overall. Those are play-action windows a veteran can hit on time. When the game turned into a catch-up passing script, the same player struggled: -0.568 EPA a play trailing by 9+, against +0.35 within one score.

The career explains why. Outside of 2017 in Minnesota (+0.174 EPA a play, 11th in the league), he has mostly lived at or below average, with negative CPOE in nearly every season and a bad-throw rate steadily in the 16-18% range. His 17% this year ranks 37th of 42, which is simply who he is. The one real skill is sack avoidance: a 3.6% sack rate, fifth-best, built on a 2.65-second time to throw that matches his history. His aggressiveness has dropped to 13.2% from the 16-17% he showed in his prime, which fits a 38-year-old playing it safe. He gets the ball out and keeps the offense on schedule. He does not stress a defense vertically: 1 of 4 on throws of 20+ yards, at -0.816 EPA a throw.

Where this heads depends on Williams' health. Williams has started every game since Week 6, and Keenum isn't even the backup. Until that changes, his numbers are frozen, and nothing in them should be projected forward.

strengths.title: Avoids sacks, plays on time
strengths.body: His 3.6% sack rate ranks fifth, and he was pressured on only 12.7% of dropbacks, also fifth. That comes from a quick, rhythm-based release (2.65 seconds) and a low-aggression approach. The pattern holds across his career, so it should carry over if he plays again.

strengths.title: Thrives under center in rhythm
strengths.body: On 14 under-center dropbacks he completed 92.9% at +0.818 EPA a play. Johnson's play-action structure did the heavy lifting there. The sample is tiny, but it matches how he won in Philadelphia: on schedule, with the offense dictating, a profile that suits a veteran backup.

strengths.title: Ran the offense cleanly vs PHI
strengths.body: His one full game produced +7.3 EPA with a 2.8 CPOE and two touchdowns, and the Bears won by 20. It came against a defense now ranked 27th, so it shows what he can do with a good script against a soft opponent. It does not set a weekly baseline.

concerns.title: Accuracy has never been his thing
concerns.body: His 17% bad-throw rate ranks 37th of 42, and his tracking CPOE is -3.27. The career shows negative CPOE in almost every season. This is a long-held trait, not a slump, and it caps what he can do when the offense asks him to carry it.

concerns.title: Falls apart in catch-up scripts
concerns.body: Trailing by 9+ he posted -0.568 EPA a play from shotgun-heavy dropbacks, with both of his sacks. The Green Bay game showed the downside: a 31.6% bad-throw rate, a pick and a lost fumble. Without the run game and play-action to lean on, he has no way to create.

concerns.title: No vertical game to speak of
concerns.body: He was 1 of 4 on throws of 20+ yards at -0.816 EPA a throw, and his aggressiveness is down to 13.2%. The Rome Odunze connection, which runs largely downfield and outside, lost 7.3 EPA on 11 targets. Kalif Raymond's underneath work gained 6.6 on 8. At 38 he is a short-to-intermediate passer only.

trend.note: Two games, opposite results: +7.3 EPA in a 20-point home win over Philadelphia, then -6.4 in partial relief at Green Bay. He hasn't thrown a pass since, with Williams starting Weeks 6 through 9.

nextGame.headline: Soft Saints pass defense, but he's QB3 and inactive.
nextGame.body:
On paper New Orleans is the kind of defense Keenum could manage. The Saints rank 22nd in pass EPA allowed and 29th in success rate. They allow 274.6 passing yards a game, 29th, and give up the most deep EPA in the league. A script where Chicago leads and runs play-action from under center would fit him well. None of that applies unless two quarterbacks ahead of him go down. He is listed as the emergency No. 3 and was inactive last week, so the realistic expectation is no snaps.

Availability on his own side would shape any appearance. Left tackle Braxton Jones is out for the season, which thins the protection his rhythm game depends on. Luther Burden, his most-targeted receiver, is questionable with a concussion. Kyle Monangai is out, weakening the run game that his under-center success rests on. For New Orleans, center Erik McCoy is out "for a little bit", and backs Travis Etienne and CJ Donaldson are sidelined. That could limit the Saints' offense and keep the game script friendly for Chicago. The Book has no line posted yet, and there's no weather data.

keyMatchups.title: Depth chart, not the defense
keyMatchups.body: Keenum is QB3 and was inactive last week. He sees the field only after injuries to the two quarterbacks ahead of him, so availability, not matchup, decides his week.

keyMatchups.title: Porous Saints coverage between the numbers
keyMatchups.body: New Orleans ranks 22nd in pass EPA, and the opposing WR1 averages 3.3 PPR over his usual output against it, 28th. Its tight-end EPA allowed ranks 28th. That would suit Keenum's short-to-intermediate, middle-of-the-field game if he were pressed into action.

keyMatchups.title: Saints' pass rush can get home
keyMatchups.body: New Orleans ranks seventh in sack rate. With Jones out, the left side is weaker, and Keenum's one reliable skill, sack avoidance, would be tested more than it was against Philadelphia.

nextGame.watch: Whether Keenum is active as the No. 2 at all. If he is, Chicago's quarterback room has changed and his outlook changes with it.

restOfSeason.body:
As the No. 3 quarterback, his expected rest-of-season production is essentially nothing: 0 to 2 attempts a game, mostly as a garbage-time or emergency body. If injuries push him back into the lineup, expect roughly what the career and this season both say. He can be efficient and sack-averse when Johnson keeps him under center with a lead, around 165 to 235 passing yards and one touchdown or so a game. He sinks when the game turns into a shotgun comeback.

The Philadelphia game is the ceiling, not the norm, and it came against a bottom-tier defense. The low sack rate is the part to trust. The accuracy and the lack of a deep game will cap him, and with Jones and possibly Burden out, the supporting cast would be thinner than in September.
